## Key terms

{{< glossary game-loop frame-rate coordinate-system origin axis coordinate ordered-pair quadrant screen-space world-space tile-grid handedness >}}

## 1.1 Mathematics in game development

A game repeats the **game loop** — read input, update the state, render — once
per **frame**. The state is only numbers, and the loop has a strict time
budget: the **frame time** is 1000 / *f* milliseconds at *f* frames per second,
so 16.7 ms at 60 fps.

![The game loop.](images/game-loop.png){width=70%}

Each area of this course answers a question the loop asks in every frame:
coordinates and vectors (*where is it, where does it go?*), trigonometry
(*which way does it face?*), matrices (*how is the model placed?*), logic
(*is the rule true?*) and probability (*what does chance decide?*).

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 1 · The frame budget"}
Choose the right value or term. Round times to one decimal place.

::: {.match extra="16.7 ms|read input|probability"}
The frame time at 30 fps.
:   33.3 ms

The frame time at 120 fps.
:   8.3 ms

The number of frames in 10 seconds at 60 fps.
:   600

The step of the loop that draws the image.
:   render

The step of the loop that applies the rules and the physics.
:   update state

The area of mathematics that decides whether a locked door opens.
:   logic
:::
:::

## 1.2 One-dimensional coordinates

On a **number line**, a point is one number: its signed distance from the
**origin**. Moving from *a* to *b* gives a **signed displacement** *b* − *a*
(the sign is the direction) and a **distance** |*b* − *a*| (never negative).
Board games use **discrete** positions (integers); physics games use
**continuous** positions (`float`). A `float` keeps about seven significant
digits, so far from the origin (around 100 000 units) positions can only
change in visible steps and objects jitter. Large worlds keep the action near
the origin with a **floating origin**.

![A runner game: the player goes back from x = 4 to the checkpoint at x = −3.](images/number-line.png){width=90%}

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 2 · Moving along a line"}
A player at *x* = 6 falls back to a checkpoint at *x* = −2.

::: {.match extra="−4"}
The player's signed displacement.
:   −8

The distance the player travels.
:   8

A platform moves from *x* = −5 to *x* = −1. Its displacement.
:   +4

The kind of number line in which a character can stand at *x* = 3.27.
:   continuous

The kind of number line used for the squares of a board game.
:   discrete

The technique that moves a large world back towards the origin.
:   floating origin
:::
:::

## 1.3 The two-dimensional Cartesian coordinate system

Two perpendicular axes meet at the origin: *x* grows to the right, *y* grows
upward. A point is an **ordered pair** (*x*, *y*) — the order matters. The
axes divide the plane into four **quadrants**, identified only by the signs of
the coordinates; a point with a zero coordinate lies on an axis.

![The four quadrants and their sign patterns.](images/quadrants.png){width=62%}

{{< sim file="sims/grid-strike.html" poster="sims/grid-strike.png" title="Grid Strike: hit the coordinates" kind="game" height="600" >}}

::: {.match extra="quadrant I|positive x-axis"}
(−5, 3)
:   quadrant II

(6, −0.5)
:   quadrant IV

(−2, −7)
:   quadrant III

(0, −4)
:   negative y-axis

The horizontal distance between (−3, 2) and (4, 2).
:   7
:::
:::

## 1.4 Screen space and world space

The screen counts **pixels from the top-left corner**, and its *y* grows
**downward**. The world counts units from an origin chosen by the designer,
with *y* upward. With the camera centred on the world origin, a screen of
*W* × *H* pixels and a scale of *s* pixels per unit:

- world → screen: *x*~s~ = *W*/2 + *s*·*x*~w~, *y*~s~ = *H*/2 − *s*·*y*~w~
- screen → world (a touch): *x*~w~ = (*x*~s~ − *W*/2) / *s*, *y*~w~ = (*H*/2 − *y*~s~) / *s*

![The same point in world space and in screen space (*s* = 100).](images/screen-world.png){width=92%}

Phones differ in resolution, so the scale is computed, not fixed: to show a
play area *w* units wide on every phone, use *s* = *W* / *w*. A taller phone
then simply shows more of the world above and below.

::: {.callout-note title="Watch out!"}
The minus sign in *y*~s~ = *H*/2 − *s*·*y*~w~ is what turns *y* around. With a
plus sign, the world is drawn upside down.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 4 · Convert between the spaces"}
A portrait phone: *W* = 1080, *H* = 1920, *s* = 100 pixels per unit, camera
centred on the world origin.

::: {.match extra="(640, 1160)|upward"}
The pixel at the centre of the screen.
:   (540, 960)

The pixel where the world point (1, 2) is drawn.
:   (640, 760)

The pixel where the world point (−3, −1) is drawn.
:   (240, 1060)

The world point touched at the pixel (740, 1360).
:   (2, −4)

The direction in which screen *y* grows.
:   downward

The scale that shows a board 9 units wide on this phone.
:   120 pixels per unit
:::
:::

## 1.5 Discrete coordinates: grids and tile maps

On a grid, a cell is a pair of integers: column *c* and row *r*, from 0.
Memory is one-dimensional, so a grid with *n* columns is stored row after row
(**row-major order**):

- index of a cell: *i* = *r* × *n* + *c*
- cell of an index: *c* = *i* mod *n* (the remainder), *r* = ⌊*i* / *n*⌋ (the whole part)

![An 8-column board: each cell has (c, r) and an index i.](images/tile-index.png){width=80%}

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 5 · A match-3 board"}
The board has 8 columns. In the last question, tiles are 2 units wide and row 0
is the bottom row.

::: {.match extra="column 2, row 3|11"}
The index of the cell in column 2, row 4.
:   34

The cell with index 19.
:   column 3, row 2

The index of the cell directly above index 19.
:   27

The index of the cell (0, 0).
:   0

The world position of the centre of tile (1, 0).
:   (3, 1)
:::
:::

## 1.6 The three-dimensional Cartesian coordinate system

A 3D point is an **ordered triple** (*x*, *y*, *z*). In a world with *y* up,
the ground is the *xz*-plane and *y* is the height. With *x* right and *y* up,
*z* can point into the screen (**left-handed**, e.g. Unity) or towards the
viewer (**right-handed**, e.g. Godot). Swapping two axes changes the
handedness: Blender (right-handed, *z* up) → Unity (left-handed, *y* up) is
(*x*, *y*, *z*) → (*x*, *z*, *y*).

![Left-handed and right-handed coordinate systems.](images/handedness.png){width=86%}

{{< sim file="sims/position-3d.html" poster="images/axes-3d.png" title="Place an object in 3D" height="640" >}}

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 6 · Positions in 3D"}
The world has *y* up unless the question says otherwise.

::: {.match extra="right-handed|(5, 1, 3)|z"}
The coordinate that gives the height.
:   y

The plane of the ground.
:   the xz-plane

Where the point (2, 0, −7) lies.
:   on the ground

The handedness of Unity's coordinate system.
:   left-handed

The Blender point (3, 1, 5) in Unity.
:   (3, 5, 1)

What swapping two axes changes.
:   the handedness
:::
:::

## Game challenge: Harbor Guard {.challenge}

Work alone. Use every section of today.

**Harbor Guard** is a portrait tower-defence game for phones (1080 × 1920
pixels, 60 fps). The camera is centred on the world origin with a scale of
120 pixels per unit. The harbour is a grid of 9 columns of tiles. The player
taps a tile to build a tower; the towers are 3D models made in Blender.

![A screen of Harbor Guard: the player taps a tile of the harbour grid.](images/harbor-guard.png){width=42%}

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 7 · Taps and ships"}
Use *s* = 120 and the screen centre (540, 960).

::: {.match extra="(2, −2)|(900, 480)"}
The frame time of the game.
:   16.7 ms

The world point touched at the pixel (300, 720).
:   (−2, 2)

The quadrant of that point.
:   quadrant II

The pixel where a ship at the world point (3, −4) is drawn.
:   (900, 1440)
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 8 · Tiles and towers (harder)"}
The harbour grid has 9 columns, stored in row-major order.

::: {.match extra="column 0, row 4|(2, 3, 1.5)"}
The index of the tile in column 4, row 6.
:   58

The tile with index 40.
:   column 4, row 4

A tower at (2, 3, 1.5) in Blender. Its position in Unity.
:   (2, 1.5, 3)

The height of that tower above the ground.
:   1.5 units
:::
:::

## Summary {.summary}

- The game loop runs once per frame; frame time = 1000 / fps ms.
- 1D: displacement *b* − *a* has a sign; distance |*b* − *a*| does not.
- 2D: ordered pair (*x*, *y*); the signs decide the quadrant.
- Screen space: pixels from the top-left, *y* down; convert with the scale *s*.
- Grids: *i* = *r* × *n* + *c*; back with mod and whole-number division.
- 3D: (*x*, *y*, *z*); left- or right-handed; swapping two axes flips it.
